issues.legal_issue: A revised agricultural ceiling is measured by the ceiling in the law currently in force, and acquisition of surplus land under that ceiling does not require market-value compensation for land within an earlier ceiling.
material_facts: The challenged legislation introduced a new ceiling on agricultural holdings and replaced the earlier ceiling.
Land was to vest in the State only to the extent it exceeded the new ceiling prescribed by the legislation.
issues.conclusion: The new ceiling was the ceiling applicable under the law for the time being in force. The second proviso to Article 31A(1) did not require market-value compensation by reference to the earlier ceiling, and the legislation was protected from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1), including its second proviso, refers to the ceiling under the law currently in force, not a ceiling under an amended or repealed earlier law. Kunjukutty v. State of Kerala and Malankara Rubber and Produce Co. v. State of Kerala applied that principle. The Court also treated the legislation as agrarian reform protected by Article 31A and, independently, by Article 31B because it was included in the Ninth Schedule; Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala was referred to in connection with the validity of a Ninth Schedule amendment.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.new_ceiling_is_current_law: The legislature replaces an earlier agricultural ceiling with a new ceiling that is in force when the acquisition occurs.
predicates.acquisition_is_confined_to_land_exceedin: The State acquires only land exceeding the ceiling prescribed by the new law.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns an agrarian ceiling law that replaces an earlier ceiling and the State acquires only land above the current ceiling, the law is protected from a challenge based on fundamental rights.

issues.legal_issue: A State enactment included in the Ninth Schedule is protected from review on the ground that it violates fundamental rights, and Parliament may provide that protection through its constituent power.
material_facts: The challenged State legislation was included in the Ninth Schedule by a constitutional amendment.
The challenge asserted that the legislation abridged fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: The legislation was protected by Article 31B from challenge on fundamental-rights grounds, and the Court could not examine its constitutionality on those grounds; legislative competence remained open to review.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B gives Ninth Schedule laws immunity from invalidation under Article 13(2). Parliament can confer that immunity by exercising its constituent power under Article 368, including for State enactments. The Court referred to Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in discussing the validity of a constitutional amendment that placed laws in the Ninth Schedule.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheduled_la: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law included in the constitutionally protected schedule.
predicates.state_enactment_is_in_ninth_schedule: A State legislature enacted the law and a constitutional amendment placed it in the Ninth Schedule.
predicates.challenge_is_based_on_fundamental_rights: The challenger alleges that the law violates or abridges fundamental rights.

issues.definition: A fundamental-rights challenge to a State law included in the protected schedule cannot be examined on its merits, although legislative competence may still be questioned.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature may define a family for agricultural-ceiling purposes and club family members’ holdings without violating the constitutional protection for land within a ceiling limit.
material_facts: The legislation defined a raiyat’s family to include specified spouses, children and other relatives, and provided for holdings of family members to be clubbed.
The definition included provision for divorced and widowed daughters in specified circumstances and allowed the ceiling area to increase with family size, subject to a maximum.
The ceiling scheme treated the individual raiyat as the unit while accounting for family members.
issues.conclusion: The family definition and clubbing provisions did not violate the second proviso to Article 31A(1); in any event, the provisions were protected by Article 31B.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14K(c) and 14M(2) were components of a law imposing a ceiling, not enlarging the maximum holding. The Court held that defining family and clubbing holdings were necessary to prevent evasion and to implement that ceiling, and that the second proviso to Article 31A(1) did not invalidate those provisions. It also relied on Article 31B as an independent protection.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.family_members_hold_land: Two or more people treated as members of a raiyat’s family hold agricultural land.
predicates.family_holdings_are_clubbed_for_a_ceilin: The legislature aggregates family members’ holdings to calculate a maximum holding and allows a limited increase based on family size.

issues.definition: Where a ceiling law aggregates family members’ holdings and allows only a capped increase based on family size, that family-based ceiling is valid against the stated constitutional challenge.

issues.legal_issue: Ceiling limits on agricultural holdings are not arbitrary merely because they vary by family size or land conditions, where they are designed for equitable distribution and account for differing agricultural circumstances.
material_facts: The legislation set different ceiling areas according to the raiyat’s family size and whether the land was irrigated or in another area.
The State had high population density and limited available land, and the legislation sought to distribute surplus land to landless people.
The Court considered differences in land productivity and local conditions and found that the prescribed limits did not substantially reduce the prior limits in the manner alleged.
issues.conclusion: The ceiling limits were reasonable and not arbitrary.
issues.legal_principle: Article 39(b) supports distribution of the community’s material resources to subserve the common good. The Court held that agrarian ceilings may account for varying local productivity and conditions and need not prescribe a uniform acreage throughout the country. It considered the ceiling provisions in section 14M and found no violation of Articles 14, 19(1)(f) or 31(2).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.ceiling_limits_account_for_family_size_o: The law sets limits that vary according to family size or relevant differences in land conditions.
predicates.surplus_land_is_intended_for_equitable_d: The law makes surplus land available for distribution to people lacking sufficient means of livelihood.

issues.definition: Ceiling limits that account for family size or land conditions and serve equitable distribution are not arbitrary on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature may disregard agricultural-land transfers made before a ceiling law takes effect when a backdated cutoff reasonably prevents evasion of the new ceiling.
material_facts: The legislation required certain transfers or partitions made during a period before publication of the ceiling law to be disregarded when calculating the holding.
A prior published legislative proposal had given landholders warning that family holdings could be considered in determining ceilings.
The Court found that transfers and partitions among family members could be used to defeat the ceiling scheme.
issues.conclusion: The backdated cutoff and the resulting treatment of the specified transfers as part of the raiyat’s holding were valid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14P used a retrospective cutoff to prevent avoidance of the ceiling law. The Court held that fixing a date before enactment is a usual legislative device and that the cutoff had a reasonable nexus to preventing anticipatory transfers and implementing the family-based ceiling. The Court also relied on the need to prevent the agrarian-reform scheme from being frustrated.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.transfers_were_made_before_the_ceiling_l: Landholders transferred or partitioned agricultural land before the ceiling law took effect.
predicates.cutoff_prevents_anticipatory_evasion: The legislature disregards transfers after a selected cutoff so that land cannot be shifted to defeat the ceiling scheme.
predicates.landholders_had_warning_of_the_proposed_: Landholders had notice of a legislative proposal relevant to the change in how holdings would be counted.

issues.definition: A backdated rule disregarding transfers is valid where it prevents anticipated evasion of a ceiling law and landholders had warning of the proposed change.

issues.legal_issue: A temporary restriction on transfers of land above an agricultural ceiling, pending determination and possession of the surplus, is a reasonable measure to implement the ceiling scheme.
material_facts: The legislation restricted a raiyat whose holding exceeded the ceiling from transferring or partitioning land while the surplus remained undetermined and unpossessed.
The restriction allowed transfers with written permission from the responsible officer.
The Court found that transfers could otherwise frustrate implementation of the ceiling scheme.
issues.conclusion: The transfer restriction was not an absolute bar and was a reasonable ancillary measure.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14U and 14P were ancillary to the agricultural ceiling scheme and necessary to prevent transfers from defeating it. The right to acquire, hold and dispose of property under Article 19(1)(f) was subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.holding_exceeds_the_ceiling: A raiyat holds more agricultural land than the applicable ceiling permits.
predicates.transfer_restriction_is_limited_until_su: The restriction lasts only until the surplus land is identified and taken into State possession.
predicates.permission_is_available: The law allows a responsible official to authorize a transfer.

issues.definition: A temporary restriction on transfers is reasonable when it applies to an over-ceiling holding only until the surplus is determined and taken, and official permission remains available.

issues.legal_issue: Land comprised in an orchard may be treated as agricultural land subject to an agricultural ceiling, with an additional allowance recognizing the reduced cultivability of orchard land.
material_facts: The legislation defined an orchard as a compact area with enough fruit-bearing trees to prevent a substantial part from being used for another agricultural purpose.
The legislation applied a ceiling to land comprised in an orchard while allowing an additional area for a raiyat, subject to the actual orchard area.
The Court found that the ordinary meaning of agricultural land included orchards.
issues.conclusion: Orchards fell within the meaning of agricultural land, and the ceiling provision with an additional allowance was valid and reasonable.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(7), 14K(e) and 14O(2) were read together. The Court interpreted agricultural land broadly enough to include orchards and held that the additional allowance reasonably reflected the fact that fruit-bearing trees prevent substantial use of the land for other cultivation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.land_is_used_as_a_fruit_tree_orchard: The land is a compact area planted with fruit-bearing trees.
predicates.orchard_trees_limit_other_cultivation: The trees prevent a substantial part of the land from being used for another agricultural purpose.
predicates.law_allows_an_orchard_adjustment: The ceiling law provides an additional allowance that accounts for the land’s orchard use.

issues.definition: Orchard land may be included in an agricultural ceiling when its use limits other cultivation and the law accounts for that use with an adjustment.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for land in an orchard acquired above the ceiling is not illusory merely because the acquisition law does not specify an orchard-specific formula, where general income-based compensation principles apply.
material_facts: The legislation provided for compensation for land vesting in the State under the ceiling scheme by reference to the general acquisition provisions.
Those provisions allowed net annual income to be calculated and compensation to be determined as a multiple of that income, using a graded scale.
The Court considered that orchard land could produce greater income than other land and that the available multiple could represent capitalized value.
issues.conclusion: The applicable compensation provisions were sufficient, and compensation for orchard land was not illusory.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14V, 16 and 17 supplied the principles and method for calculating compensation, including computation of net annual income and application of a graded multiple. The Court held that, after the Fourth Amendment, the amount of compensation was not justiciable where the legislature had prescribed principles for its computation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_ceiling_land: A person brings a constitutional challenge to acquisition of land under an agricultural ceiling law.
predicates.orchard_land_vests_as_surplus: Land used as an orchard is acquired because it exceeds the applicable ceiling.
predicates.general_compensation_rules_apply_by_net_: The applicable compensation scheme calculates compensation by reference to the land’s net annual income.
predicates.compensation_is_computed_under_prescribe: The legislature has prescribed principles and a method for calculating compensation.

issues.definition: Compensation for acquired orchard land is not illusory where general prescribed rules calculate it by reference to net annual income.

issues.legal_issue: The inclusion of a homestead in an agricultural holding does not require invalidation of a ceiling law where the holder may retain it within the ceiling and compensation is available if it vests.
material_facts: The law included a homestead where it formed part of an agricultural holding in the record of rights.
A raiyat could retain land, including a homestead, within the applicable ceiling.
A homestead recorded as non-agricultural land or part of a non-agricultural holding did not fall within the law.
The Court found that compensation could be calculated under the general provisions if a homestead vested in the State.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a separate homestead-compensation provision did not invalidate the law; a raiyat could retain a homestead within the ceiling, and compensation was available if it vested.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(7), 14M, 14V and 16(1)(a)(ii), together with rules 15(b) and 15(d), governed homesteads included in agricultural holdings and the calculation of compensation. The Court relied on the holder’s ability to retain the homestead within the ceiling and on the applicable compensation procedure for land that vested.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_ceiling_land: A person brings a constitutional challenge to acquisition of land under an agricultural ceiling law.
predicates.homestead_is_part_of_an_agricultural_hol: The homestead is recorded as part of an agricultural holding.
predicates.holder_can_retain_homestead_within_ceili: The landholder may choose to keep the homestead within the applicable ceiling area.
predicates.compensation_procedure_applies_if_homest: The law provides a method for calculating compensation if the homestead nevertheless vests in the State.

issues.definition: A ceiling law is not invalid for lacking a separate homestead-compensation provision when the holder may retain an agricultural homestead within the ceiling and compensation applies if it vests.

issues.legal_issue: Attributing a private trust’s land to its beneficiaries for ceiling calculations does not violate the right of religious or charitable bodies to manage their affairs where the State’s eminent-domain power applies and safeguards allow additional land for qualifying purposes.
material_facts: The legislation treated land owned by a private trust or endowment as held by its beneficiaries to the extent of their beneficial interests.
The resulting ceiling could reduce the trust’s landholding.
The State could increase the ceiling where land, rather than merely its income, was needed to perform an exclusively charitable or religious obligation.
issues.conclusion: The trust-land provision did not violate Article 26; the State’s power of eminent domain applied, and the statutory power to increase the ceiling provided a safeguard for qualifying trusts and institutions.
issues.legal_principle: Article 26 does not remove property from the State’s inherent power of eminent domain. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh and applied sections 14M(5) and 14O(3), which attributed private-trust land to beneficiaries for ceiling purposes while allowing an increased ceiling where land was required for an exclusively charitable or religious purpose.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_private_trus: A person challenges the application of an agricultural ceiling to land held by a private trust or endowment.
predicates.trust_land_is_attributed_to_beneficiarie: The law counts trust land as held by beneficiaries according to their beneficial interests.
predicates.state_can_exercise_eminent_domain: The State has power to acquire property for a public purpose.

issues.definition: Attributing private-trust land to beneficiaries for a ceiling does not violate religious or charitable rights where eminent domain applies and an increased allowance is available for qualifying land needs.
